title: Greece emergency call and 112 alert quick card
summary: Use 112 free of charge in Greece or elsewhere in the EU when immediate emergency assistance is required.
content: 112 connects urgent incidents with the appropriate emergency services. Call only for a real emergency. Give your exact location, what happened, current hazards, and how many people may need help. Follow the operator’s instructions and keep the line available.
steps: Move away from immediate danger if you can do so safely.
Call 112 and state the location first.
Describe the incident, hazards, number of people, and urgent symptoms.
Answer questions clearly and follow instructions.
Do not end the call until the operator says you may, unless remaining connected creates danger.
warnings: Do not make unnecessary calls to 112.
Do not enter fire, floodwater, unstable structures, traffic, or electrical hazards to obtain a better view.
common_mistakes: Giving a long story before the location.
Assuming the operator already knows the exact apartment, floor, rural road, beach, or trail position.
alternatives: If a voice call is impossible, use another available phone or ask a nearby person to contact 112 while you maintain safety.
failure_signs: The call drops, the location is uncertain, conditions worsen, or a new hazard blocks access.
when_not_to_use: Do not use 112 for routine information, non-urgent complaints, or test calls.
short_term: Keep the route clear for responders and assign someone to guide them from a safe point.
long_term: Store your address, building access details, medical needs, and emergency contacts offline and rehearse a concise emergency report.
if_method_fails: Move to a safer reception area if possible, retry, ask another person to call, and use any locally available emergency channel.
environment_notes: In remote, island, mountain, coastal, or construction locations, provide landmarks, access restrictions, gate codes, floor level, and visible hazards.

title: Household emergency plan and supply kit
summary: Prepare several days of water, food, medicines, light, communication, hygiene, documents, and a family contact plan.
content: A useful kit supports drinking, sanitation, essential medication, lighting, communication, and evacuation without depending on immediate shops or utilities. Ready.gov recommends one gallon of water per person per day for several days; this project rounds that to about 4 litres per person per day.
materials: about 4 litres of water per person per day for several days
non-perishable food and manual can opener
torch, batteries, radio, power banks and charging cables
copies of identification, contacts and key documents
steps: List household members, pets, medicines, mobility needs, and equipment that depends on power.
Choose meeting points and an out-of-area contact.
Pack supplies in portable containers and label dates.
Store additional supplies at home where heat, water, and pests will not damage them.
Review water, food, batteries, medicines, and documents on a fixed schedule.
warnings: Water needs increase with heat, heavy work, illness, pregnancy, breastfeeding, children, pets, and sanitation demands.
Do not store fuel, loose chemicals, or leaking batteries with food, water, or medicines.
common_mistakes: Buying equipment without practising with it.
Forgetting prescriptions, glasses, hearing-aid batteries, chargers, pet carriers, or accessibility equipment.
alternatives: Build the kit gradually, starting with water, medicines, light, communication, and documents.
failure_signs: Expired items, damaged containers, dead batteries, missing medicines, or a plan no household member can explain.
when_not_to_use: Do not delay an ordered evacuation to finish packing.
short_term: Create a minimum 72-hour kit and a written contact/meeting plan.
long_term: Expand supplies according to local hazards and rotate them before expiry.
if_method_fails: Take the highest-priority available items: medicines, phone, identification, water, weather protection, keys, and evacuation information.
environment_notes: Adapt for apartments, vehicles, ferries, islands, rural roads, heat, winter weather, construction work, pets, and power-dependent medical equipment.

title: Earthquake immediate actions
summary: Protect yourself from falling objects during shaking, then check for injuries, fire, leaks, structural damage, and official instructions.
content: During strong shaking, the immediate priority is protection from falling glass, furniture, masonry, and electrical hazards. After shaking stops, expect aftershocks and do not re-enter a visibly damaged structure until authorities or qualified professionals consider it safe.
steps: If indoors, stay inside, move away from windows and tall unsecured objects, drop low, cover your head and neck, and hold on to sturdy shelter if available.
If outdoors, move to an open area away from buildings, walls, signs, trees, and power lines.
When shaking stops, check yourself and others, put on shoes, and watch for debris.
If you smell gas, see fire, sparking, damaged wiring, or major structural damage, move away without operating switches or flames.
Use stairs rather than lifts and follow official instructions.
warnings: Aftershocks can cause additional collapse.
Do not enter damaged buildings or touch fallen electrical lines.
common_mistakes: Running through falling debris during shaking.
Standing in doorways without knowing whether they provide protection.
Using a lift after the earthquake.
alternatives: If no sturdy table is nearby, get low beside an interior wall away from glass and protect the head and neck.
failure_signs: Cracking or leaning walls, falling masonry, fire, gas odour, sparking, jammed doors, or repeated aftershocks.
when_not_to_use: Do not remain under visibly failing ceilings or beside fire, gas, chemical, or electrical hazards.
short_term: Account for people, treat immediate injuries within your training, and move to a safe assembly point if evacuation is necessary.
long_term: Secure furniture, identify utility shutoffs, store supplies, and practise household earthquake actions.
if_method_fails: Choose the nearest position that reduces exposure to falling objects and protect the head and neck until movement becomes safer.
environment_notes: On the coast, follow official tsunami instructions after strong or long shaking. In construction sites, avoid cranes, scaffolds, excavations, suspended loads, and partially completed structures.

title: Flood route and electrical safety
summary: Move away from underground and low areas, never cross moving water, avoid electrical hazards, and return only when authorities say it is safe.
content: Floodwater can hide missing road surfaces, open drains, contamination, current, and energized equipment. Greek Civil Protection advises moving to a secure higher point, not crossing torrents on foot or by car, and changing direction when a road is flooded.
steps: Follow warnings early and limit travel.
Leave basements, underground parking, stream beds, and other low areas.
Move to a secure higher point using a route that is not flooded.
Stop and change direction at flooded roads or crossings.
Stay away from wires, substations, damaged electrical equipment, and stagnant water near possible electrical faults.
Return only after official clearance and inspect utilities before use.
warnings: Do not walk or drive through moving water or torrents.
Floodwater may be contaminated and may conceal sharp objects, holes, and unstable ground.
common_mistakes: Assuming a familiar road or shallow-looking crossing is safe.
Entering a basement to save property after water begins rising.
alternatives: Use a preselected higher route or remain at a safe upper level while contacting emergency services if all exits are hazardous.
failure_signs: Rapidly rising water, moving debris, vehicle loss of traction, current around legs, sparking, sewage odour, or unstable ground.
when_not_to_use: Do not attempt property recovery, pumping, or electrical restoration while water is present or the structure is unassessed.
short_term: Reach a safe higher location, report trapped or missing people, and avoid contaminated water.
long_term: Map flood history, safe high points, blocked-drain risks, and routes that do not cross torrents.
if_method_fails: Stop movement, retreat to the last secure point, call 112, and make your location visible without entering the water.
environment_notes: Urban underpasses, basement garages, island roads, river crossings, and construction excavations can fill rapidly.

title: Wildfire warning and evacuation readiness
summary: Prevent ignition, report fire immediately, prepare the property before danger, and strictly follow official relocation instructions and routes.
content: Wildfire conditions can change faster than a household can react. Keep access clear, remove dry vegetation and flammable material according to local rules, prepare transport and essential supplies, and leave promptly when authorities order relocation.
steps: During high-risk periods, avoid outdoor burning, sparks, and open flames near dry vegetation.
If you see a fire, call 199 or 112 immediately and report the exact location, direction, and vegetation involved.
Keep gates and access routes available for emergency vehicles.
Prepare people, pets, medicines, documents, and transport before smoke or flame blocks routes.
If organised relocation is ordered, follow the authorities’ route and timing without delay.
warnings: Do not wait for visible flames before acting on an evacuation order.
Do not drive into dense smoke or use an unconfirmed route.
common_mistakes: Returning for property after evacuation begins.
Blocking access with vehicles or hoses.
Relying on a single exit route.
alternatives: If the planned route is blocked, use the official alternate route or contact 112 from the safest available shelter; do not improvise through fire or dense smoke.
failure_signs: Ash or embers, falling visibility, strong radiant heat, blocked roads, power loss, or official alerts naming your area.
when_not_to_use: Do not remain to defend property without training, suitable equipment, safe water supply, and a fully secure escape route.
short_term: Move early, account for everyone, and keep roads clear for emergency services.
long_term: Maintain defensible space and evacuation routes within applicable law and review the plan before each fire season.
if_method_fails: Use the safest substantial shelter available, close openings against smoke and embers where appropriate, call 112, and follow live official instructions.
environment_notes: Wind, slope, dry vegetation, narrow island or village roads, and smoke can remove escape options quickly.

title: Emergency drinking-water safety
summary: Use bottled or officially approved water first; boiling kills germs but does not remove chemicals, fuel, salt, or radioactive contamination.
content: When water safety is uncertain, follow the local advisory. For microbial contamination, CDC guidance says to bring clear water to a full rolling boil for 1 minute, or 3 minutes above about 2,000 metres, then cool it naturally and store it in a clean covered container. Boiling does not remove chemicals.
materials: clean cloth or coffee filter for cloudy water
steps: Check the official advisory and identify whether the problem is germs, chemicals, salt, fuel, or another contaminant.
Use bottled water when authorities recommend it.
For germ contamination only, let cloudy water settle or filter it through a clean cloth, then boil the clearer water.
Maintain a full rolling boil for 1 minute; above about 2,000 metres, boil for 3 minutes.
Cool without adding ice and store in a clean, sanitized, tightly covered container.
warnings: Boiling does not remove chemicals, petroleum, salt, heavy metals, or radioactive material.
Do not use floodwater or water with fuel, chemical, unusual colour, or unusual odour unless authorities specifically declare a safe treatment.
common_mistakes: Assuming a household filter makes advisory water safe without boiling.
Adding unsafe ice after boiling.
Touching the inside of clean lids or containers.
alternatives: Use sealed bottled water or an authority-approved treatment method appropriate to the identified contaminant.
failure_signs: Continuing official prohibition, chemical odour, oily film, illness, damaged well, sewage intrusion, or inability to maintain clean storage.
when_not_to_use: Do not apply boiling as the only treatment when chemical, fuel, saltwater, or radioactive contamination is suspected.
short_term: Protect a clearly marked supply for drinking, food preparation, medicine, infant feeding, toothbrushing, and pet needs.
long_term: Store and rotate emergency water and keep containers away from fuel, pesticides, heat, and sunlight.
if_method_fails: Stop using the source, isolate it, switch to bottled or officially supplied water, and seek public-health guidance.
environment_notes: Water needs rise during heat, physical work, illness, pregnancy, breastfeeding, and when sanitation systems fail.

title: Food safety during a power outage
summary: Keep appliance doors closed: an unopened refrigerator is generally safe for up to 4 hours, a full freezer for 48 hours, and a half-full freezer for 24 hours.
content: Time and temperature determine food safety; smell and appearance are not reliable tests. CDC guidance gives the 4-hour refrigerator, 48-hour full-freezer, and 24-hour half-full-freezer limits when doors remain closed.
materials: paper and pen for outage time
steps: Record when power was lost and keep refrigerator and freezer doors closed.
After 4 hours, move refrigerated perishables to a cooler at 4°C or below if a cold source is available.
Use an appliance thermometer to verify food temperature when possible.
Discard perishable refrigerated food that has been above 4°C for 2 hours or more, or 1 hour in very hot conditions, following official guidance.
When uncertain, discard the food rather than tasting it.
warnings: Never taste food to decide whether it is safe.
Discard food contaminated by floodwater, sewage, chemicals, damaged packaging, or unsafe temperatures.
common_mistakes: Opening doors repeatedly.
Relying on smell, taste, or appearance.
Refreezing thawed food without checking temperature and ice crystals.
alternatives: Use shelf-stable food that requires little or no water and heat.
failure_signs: Unknown outage duration, temperature above safe limits, leaking packages, swelling cans, unusual texture, or flood exposure.
when_not_to_use: Do not serve uncertain food to infants, pregnant people, older adults, immunocompromised people, or anyone else.
short_term: Prioritise safe foods, label discard decisions, and protect drinking water from cross-contamination.
long_term: Keep thermometers in appliances, freeze water containers to add thermal mass, and plan shelf-stable meals.
if_method_fails: Discard uncertain perishables and switch to sealed shelf-stable food and safe water.
environment_notes: Outage times shorten when doors are opened, appliances start warm, or the surrounding temperature is high.

title: Generator and carbon monoxide safety
summary: Run fuel-burning generators only outdoors, more than 20 feet (about 6 metres) from windows, doors, and vents, with exhaust directed away.
content: Carbon monoxide is colourless and odourless. CDC guidance says never use a generator inside a home or garage, even with doors or windows open, and to place it outdoors more than 20 feet from openings.
materials: dry weather protection that preserves ventilation
steps: Place the generator outdoors, more than about 6 metres from windows, doors, and vents.
Point exhaust away from buildings and occupied areas.
Keep it dry without enclosing it or blocking airflow.
Use the manufacturer’s connection method; never back-feed a building through a wall outlet.
Install and test CO alarms near sleeping areas and on occupied levels.
Shut down and cool the generator before refuelling.
warnings: Never operate a generator in a house, garage, basement, shed, balcony enclosure, stairwell, or near open windows.
Headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, chest pain, confusion, or collapse may indicate carbon monoxide poisoning; move to fresh air and call 112.
common_mistakes: Assuming an open garage door provides enough ventilation.
Placing the generator close to a neighbour’s window or shared air intake.
Refuelling while hot.
alternatives: Use charged power banks, battery lighting, or professionally installed backup systems for essential low-power needs.
failure_signs: CO alarm activation, exhaust entering a building, unstable operation, fuel leak, damaged cable, overheating, or symptoms in any person.
when_not_to_use: Do not use the generator when safe outdoor clearance, dry operation, correct cabling, or competent supervision cannot be maintained.
short_term: Stop the engine, move everyone to fresh air, and call 112 if exposure is suspected.
long_term: Arrange qualified electrical installation, maintain the generator, rotate fuel legally and safely, and test CO alarms monthly.
if_method_fails: Disconnect the load and stop using the generator; switch to non-combustion backup power or evacuate to a powered safe location.
environment_notes: Shared apartment courtyards, balconies, tents, caravans, construction cabins, and partially enclosed spaces can accumulate exhaust.

title: Heat illness recognition and escalation
summary: Confusion, altered speech, loss of consciousness, seizures, or very high body temperature suggest heat stroke and require immediate emergency care.
content: Heat stroke can cause permanent disability or death. Call 112, move the person to shade or a cool area, remove excess outer clothing, and cool rapidly while emergency help is coming. Do not give fluids to a person who is confused, unconscious, seizing, or unable to swallow safely.
steps: Stop work or exercise and move the person out of heat.
Call 112 immediately for confusion, altered speech, collapse, seizure, or suspected heat stroke.
Remove excess outer clothing and start rapid cooling with cool water, wet cloths, airflow, or a cold-water/ice bath when safely available.
Stay with the person and monitor breathing and responsiveness.
For milder heat exhaustion in an alert person, cool them and offer frequent small sips of cool water while arranging medical evaluation if symptoms are severe or do not improve.
warnings: Do not leave a confused or unconscious person alone.
Do not force fluids into anyone who cannot swallow safely.
Do not stop or change regular medication without medical advice.
common_mistakes: Waiting for sweating to stop before treating heat stroke.
Sending the person back to work after brief improvement.
Using alcohol or very sugary drinks for rehydration.
alternatives: Move to an air-conditioned public or private location and use available cool water and wet cloths while waiting for help.
failure_signs: Worsening confusion, collapse, seizure, breathing difficulty, chest pain, inability to drink, or no improvement with cooling.
when_not_to_use: Do not treat suspected heat stroke as simple dehydration or delay emergency care to measure temperature.
short_term: Continue cooling and monitoring until emergency services take over.
long_term: Plan work/rest cycles, acclimatisation, shade, water access, buddy checks, and medication review for heat exposure.
if_method_fails: Escalate immediately to 112 and use the fastest safe cooling method available while maintaining airway safety.
environment_notes: Risk rises with construction work, protective clothing, humidity, direct sun, poor airflow, chronic illness, some medicines, and lack of acclimatisation.

title: Poisoning response and Greek Poison Centre
summary: For severe symptoms or immediate danger call 112; Greece’s Poison Centre provides free 24/7 information at 210 7793777.
content: The Greek Ministry of Health states that the national Poison Centre operates 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, and provides information free of charge at 210 7793777. Keep the product container, label, medicine package, or a photo available, but do not delay emergency action.
materials: fresh air or clean-water access only when safe
steps: Move away from an active chemical, smoke, or gas hazard without exposing yourself.
Call 112 for breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure, severe confusion, chest pain, major burns, or immediate danger.
Call the Greek Poison Centre at 210 7793777 for poisoning information.
State the person’s age, symptoms, substance, amount, time, route of exposure, and actions already taken.
Follow professional instructions exactly and keep the container or label available.
warnings: Do not induce vomiting or give food, drink, charcoal, medicine, or a chemical neutraliser unless a qualified professional specifically instructs it.
Do not enter a contaminated area without appropriate training and protection.
common_mistakes: Waiting for symptoms before calling.
Mixing cleaning chemicals.
Discarding the package or forgetting the exposure time.
alternatives: Ask another person to call while you maintain airway safety or move to fresh air, but avoid contaminating yourself or others.
failure_signs: Breathing difficulty, worsening drowsiness, collapse, seizure, burns, repeated vomiting, chest pain, or multiple exposed people.
when_not_to_use: Do not rely on online or offline text instead of immediate professional advice for an actual poisoning.
short_term: Maintain safety, preserve evidence of the substance, and monitor breathing and responsiveness while help is arranged.
long_term: Store medicines and chemicals in original labelled containers, separated from food and inaccessible to children.
if_method_fails: Call 112, move to a safe location, and seek immediate emergency medical care.
environment_notes: Chemical incidents in enclosed rooms, wells, tanks, garages, construction areas, and fires may also endanger rescuers.
